title: Aftershock zones of 148 isolated Japanese Mj 5+ earthquakes grew 1.46 times in 0.01-10 days after background control (JMA 1999-2024); later growth was background; ETAS cascades can explain it
abstract: We tested if aftershock zones grow with time when background events, sample size and early detection loss are controlled. We used the JMA unified hypocenter catalog (1998-2024) and isolated mainshocks of Mj 5.0 or more at depths of 60 km or less. We stacked epicentral distances in units of the rupture length L, subtracted a pre-mainshock background, and used within-sequence permutations and a bootstrap over sequences. Without background control, the stacked median distance increased from 0.44 L to 1.80 L over 0.01-316 days. But the expected background share was 0.39 at 10-32 days and 0.99 at 100-316 days, and the background-subtracted median stayed between 0.41 L and 0.53 L. Thus the catalog cannot resolve growth after about 10 days for these sequences. In 0.01-10 days (148 sequences, 3,761 events, background share 0.09 or less), the median distance increased from 0.38 L to 0.57 L. The ratio was 1.46 (95% CI 1.19-1.92, permutation p = 0.001), and the share of events within 1 L decreased from 0.83 to 0.65. The growth stayed in 14 of 17 variants, including declustering, a higher magnitude cut, the JMA high-precision flag only, along-axis distance, inland and offshore sets, and both depth classes. It was not significant with Mth = Mj - 2, with a start at 0.1 day, or in 1999-2010. Log-time growth and a curve that saturates near 1 day fit equally well (AIC 6.1). Diffusion fit less well (AIC 12.3). ETAS simulations with a fixed primary kernel gave growth ratios of 0.98-1.11 for branching ratio 0.3, 1.02-1.27 for 0.6 and 1.03-1.53 for 0.9. Thus near-critical cascades can make the observed growth without afterslip. Limitations: generic L scaling, offshore location errors, mostly offshore sequences, and an ETAS grid that was not fitted to these sequences.
